nghe.t: Part 1. You will hear a woman talking to a librarian about joining a public library. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 10.
Good afternoon. Welcome to Westbrook Library. How can I help you?
Hello. I've just moved to this area and I'd like to join the library. Can I do that today?
Of course. It only takes a few minutes. I just need to fill in a form with you. Can I have your name, please?
Yes, it's Sara Marlow.
Could you spell your surname for me?
Sure. It's M, A, R, L, O, W.
M, A, R, L, O, W. Thank you. And what's your address, Sara?
It's 27 Canal Street.
Is that K, A, N…?
No, it starts with a C. C, A, N, A, L. Canal Street. It's near the station.
Oh yes, I know it. 27 Canal Street. And can I have a phone number?
My mobile number is 07700 900 462.
07700 900 462. Good. Now, are you a student? We have a special card for students.
Not any more. I finished university last year. I'm a nurse now, at the city hospital.
A nurse. Lovely. Now, I need to see something with your address on it. Have you got a letter from your bank, for example?
I haven't got a bank letter with me, I'm afraid. But I've got a phone bill here. Is that all right?
Yes, a phone bill is fine. Thank you. Now, joining the library is free. You only pay if you lose your card and need a new one. That used to be two pounds, but now it's three pounds.
Three pounds. OK. I'll try not to lose it! How many books can I take home?
With an adult card, you can borrow eight books at one time. Children can only take four.
Eight is plenty for me. And how long can I keep them?
You can keep books for three weeks. But be careful with films. DVDs are only for one week.
Three weeks for books. Right. What time do you close? I usually finish work at six.
On most days we close at half past five, I'm afraid. But on Thursday we stay open late, until eight in the evening.
Oh, good. So Thursday is the best day for me. Are you open at the weekend?
We're open on Saturday morning, until one o'clock. We're closed on Sunday.
OK. One last question. Do you have any classes here? My friend told me about a Spanish class.
We did have a Spanish class, but it finished last month. At the moment, there is a free computer class for members. It's on Monday mornings at ten o'clock.
A computer class. My mother would love that. I'll tell her about it.
Please do. Right, here is your card, Sara. Welcome to Westbrook Library.
Thank you very much.

nghe.t: Part 2. You will hear a woman from a bus company talking to local people about changes to bus services and about a new bus station. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 20.

Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name is Karen Wells, and I work for Riverton City Buses. I'm here to tell you about some changes to our bus services. They all begin on Monday the third of June.

Let me start with the biggest change. As you may know, we are moving to a new bus station on Station Road. Some people think we are doing this to save money. That isn't true. The new building is actually costing us a lot. The real reason is that the old station on Market Street is too small. It was built for ten bus routes, and today we have eighteen.

Now, a few words about the number 7 bus, because many of you use it. It will still run every fifteen minutes, and the first bus will still leave at six in the morning. What is new is that the number 7 will stop at the City Hospital. Patients and visitors have asked for this for years.

Next, tickets. At the moment, a single ticket costs one pound eighty. From June, if you pay the driver, a single ticket will cost two pounds. But if you buy your ticket with our phone app, you will pay only one pound fifty. So the app is the cheapest way to travel.

There is good news for families, too. People over sixty-five already travel free every day, and that is not changing. Students will continue to pay half price. The new offer is for children. From June, children under twelve will travel free at weekends when they are with an adult.

Finally, timetables. The new timetable is on our website now. If you would like a paper copy, please don't go to the old bus station, because the office there has already closed. From next week, you can pick up a timetable at the public library. People often ask at the tourist office, but they don't have them.

Now, let me describe the new bus station, so that you can find your way around. Please look at the plan. You come in through the main entrance from Station Road. The information desk is straight in front of you, in the middle of the hall.

The ticket office is very easy to find. It's immediately on your right as you come in. On your left, opposite the ticket office, there will be a small newspaper shop, but that won't open until the autumn.

If you are hungry, walk past the information desk towards the bus stops. The café is in the far left corner of the hall, right next to the bus stops. In the other corner, on the far right, there is an office for our drivers. That is not open to the public.

The waiting room is on the right-hand side of the hall, about halfway between the entrance and the bus stops. It has seats for sixty people, and it is heated in winter. The toilets are directly opposite the waiting room, on the left-hand side of the hall.

One more thing. Many of you come by bike. The bicycle park is outside the building. When you stand on Station Road and look at the main entrance, it is on your left. Taxis wait on the other side, to the right of the entrance. Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?

nghe.t: Part 3. You will hear two students, Maya and Ben, choosing a topic for a presentation on their City Life course. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 30.
Hi, Maya. Have you got a minute? We need to choose a topic for our presentation for Dr Hall.
Yes, good idea. The course is called City Life, so the topic has to be about a problem or a place in our city.
Right. How long does the presentation have to be? I thought it was fifteen minutes.
No, fifteen minutes was last term. This time we only have ten minutes, and then the class can ask questions.
Ten minutes. OK, that isn't long. So, what about traffic? There is a lot of information about it online.
That's true, and it isn't a difficult topic. But I talked to some people in our class yesterday, and four other pairs are already doing traffic. Dr Hall will be bored.
You're right. We need something different.
What about recycling? I think it's really interesting.
It is interesting, but I did a big project on recycling at secondary school. I don't want to do the same thing again.
Fair enough. Well, how about parks? We could talk about Victoria Park. Who uses it, and how can we make it better?
I like that. Nobody else is doing parks. Let's go there together and look around. Are you free on Friday afternoon?
No, sorry. I have a class until five on Friday. What about Saturday morning?
Saturday morning is fine. I can't do Sunday anyway, because I work in a café.
Great. So, who is doing what? First, we need some photos of the park.
I'll take the photos. My phone has a really good camera.
Good, because mine is terrible. We should also ask people some questions. Why do they come to the park? How often? We need a questionnaire.
I can write it if you like.
Actually, I'd like to write the questionnaire. I made one for my psychology course last year, so I know how to do it.
OK, the questionnaire is yours. What about the slides?
Let's make the slides together. We can meet in the library on Monday.
Perfect. Now, let's plan the talk. How should we start?
I think we should begin with a short history of the park. It opened in 1890, you know. Just one minute, with an old photo.
Nice. Then the main part is our results. Why do people visit the park? Shall we put the numbers in a table?
A table is a bit boring, and it's hard to read from the back of the room. Let's use a chart. Everyone can understand a chart quickly.
OK, a chart. And at the end, we should give one idea for improving the park. I was going to say more lights, because it's dark in the evening.
Lights are a good idea, but I think seats are more important. There are only six in the whole park, and old people have nowhere to sit.
That's a good point. Let's say the park needs more seats, then.
Great. I'll write the plan tonight and send it to you.

nghe.t: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about sleep. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Good morning, everyone. In today's talk, I want to look at something that we all do every night, but that most of us know very little about: sleep.

Let's begin with a simple fact. An average person spends about a third of their life asleep. So if you live to the age of ninety, you will sleep for about thirty years. That sounds like a waste of time. But, as we will see, it isn't.

How much sleep do we need? For most adults, the answer is between seven and nine hours a night. Teenagers need more than adults, up to ten hours, because their bodies and brains are still growing. And a new baby may sleep for sixteen hours a day.

Now, sleep is not the same all through the night. We sleep in cycles, and each cycle lasts about ninety minutes. In a normal night, you go through four or five of these cycles. Each cycle has several stages. I will describe the two most important ones.

The first is deep sleep. In deep sleep, your breathing is slow, and it is very difficult to wake you. This is the time when the body repairs its muscles after the work of the day. That is why sports players need plenty of sleep.

The second stage is dream sleep. Scientists call it REM sleep. In this stage, your body does not move, but your eyes move quickly under your eyelids. The brain is very busy. It goes through the information from the day, and it stores new memories. So, if you study in the evening and then sleep well, you will remember more the next day.

What happens when we do not get enough sleep? First, it becomes hard to concentrate, and we make more mistakes at work or at school. Our health suffers, too. Studies show that people who sleep for less than six hours a night catch more colds than people who sleep well.
And there is a serious danger on the roads. Tired drivers react slowly, and they cause thousands of accidents every year.
So, how can we sleep better? Here is some simple advice. First, go to bed at the same time every night, even at weekends. Your body likes a routine.
Second, be careful about what you drink. Do not drink coffee after lunch, because caffeine stays in the body for many hours. A cup of warm milk in the evening is fine.

Third, think about your bedroom. It should be dark and quiet. Many people think that a warm bedroom helps you to sleep. In fact, the opposite is true. The room should be cool. About eighteen degrees is best.
And finally, switch off your phone at least half an hour before bed. Next week, we will look at dreams, and at what they can tell us. Thank you.

nhom.huongDan: Passage 1 — Câu 1–4. Complete the sentences below. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 1
THE STORY OF THE TRAFFIC LIGHT
The signal that controls our streets is older than the car

Every day, millions of drivers, cyclists and pedestrians stop and go because of three coloured lights. Traffic lights are so common that most of us hardly notice them. It may be surprising to learn, then, that the first traffic signal is more than 150 years old. In fact, it was built before the car was even invented.
In the 1860s, the streets of London were crowded with horses, carriages and people on foot, and accidents were common. A railway engineer called John Peake Knight had an idea. He suggested that the city should use a signal like the ones on the railways. In December 1868, his signal was put up outside the Houses of Parliament. During the day, it had long arms that moved up and down to tell traffic when to stop. At night, when the arms could not be seen, it showed red and green gas lamps instead. A police officer stood beside the signal and changed it by hand. Unfortunately, the experiment ended badly. Early in 1869, gas escaped from the signal and it exploded, and the police officer was badly hurt. The signal was soon taken away, and London did not try the idea again for many years.
The next steps were taken in the United States, where the number of cars was growing fast. In 1914, one of the first electric traffic signals was installed at a busy street corner in Cleveland, Ohio. It had only two colours, red and green. It also had a buzzer, which made a loud noise to warn drivers that the lights were about to change. However, two colours were not enough. Drivers could not see any warning before the light turned red, so many of them could not stop in time. In 1920, a police officer in Detroit named William Potts solved this problem by adding a third light, yellow, between the red and the green. The yellow light showed drivers that the red light was coming. His signal could also control traffic coming from four directions at the same time, and other cities soon copied it.
These early electric signals still needed a person to operate them. During the 1920s, engineers began to add timers, so that the lights changed automatically after a fixed number of seconds. This saved money, because cities no longer had to pay police officers to stand at every crossing. But timers had one weakness: people sometimes had to wait at a red light although the other road was completely empty. Later, engineers found an answer. They placed sensors under the surface of the road. These sensors can tell when a vehicle is waiting, so the lights change only when it is necessary.
People on foot needed signals of their own. The first ones simply showed words such as "WALK" and "DON'T WALK". Later, many countries replaced the words with pictures: a red figure standing still and a green figure walking. Pictures are easier for children to understand, and also for visitors who cannot read the local language. The most famous figure comes from East Berlin. In 1961, a traffic psychologist called Karl Peglau designed a little man wearing a hat, known in German as the "Ampelmann". After Germany became one country again in 1990, the government planned to replace him with the standard figure used in the west. Many people protested, however, and the little man was saved. Today, his picture appears on T-shirts, bags and cups in souvenir shops all over Berlin.
Traffic lights are still changing today. Many now have a countdown display, which shows how many seconds are left before the light changes. Some make a sound, so that blind people know when it is safe to cross. The old light bulbs have been replaced by LED lamps, which use much less electricity and last for many years. In some cities, the lights are connected to a central computer. Using cameras, the computer watches the traffic and changes the timing of the lights to keep vehicles moving. Engineers are even testing systems in which cars and traffic lights can send messages to each other. Whatever happens in the future, however, the three colours – red, yellow and green – will probably stay with us.

READING PASSAGE 2
TURNING THE CLASSROOM UPSIDE DOWN
In a "flipped" classroom, students meet new ideas at home and practise them at school

In a traditional lesson, the teacher stands at the front of the room and explains a new topic. The students listen and take notes. Later, at home, they practise alone by doing homework. This pattern has hardly changed for more than a hundred years. In a "flipped classroom", however, the order is turned upside down. Students first meet new ideas at home, usually by watching a short video. Class time is then used for practice, with the teacher there to help.
The idea became widely known after 2007, when two teachers at a school in Colorado, in the United States, began to record their chemistry lessons. At first, the recordings were only for students who had been absent. But the teachers soon noticed something interesting: students who had been in class were watching the videos too, because they wanted to go over the lesson again. Since then, schools in many countries have tried the method.
How does a flipped lesson work? David Osei, who teaches maths at Brookside School in the north of England, describes his week. First, he records a video of about ten minutes and puts it on the school website. At home, his students watch the video. They can stop it or repeat any part, and they write down any questions they have. They then complete a short online quiz. Before the lesson, Mr Osei looks at the results of the quiz to see which points were difficult. In class, there is a short discussion of the students' questions. After that, the students solve problems in small groups, while the teacher walks around the room and helps anyone who is stuck. Finally, the students write a summary of what they have learned in their notebooks.
Mr Osei says the biggest change is in how he uses his time. "I used to talk for forty minutes while thirty students sat in silence," he says. "Now I speak to every student at least once in each lesson." He admits, however, that the method was hard work at the start. "In the first year, I spent most of my weekends making videos," he says.
The students have noticed a difference too. Sofia Rossi, who is fifteen, likes being able to watch the difficult parts again. "In a normal lesson, I was too shy to ask the teacher to repeat something," she explains. "With a video, I can play it three times and nobody knows." But she adds that the system only works if everyone prepares. "Some of my classmates don't watch the videos," she says, "and then they can't join in the group work."
The head teacher of Brookside, Helen Marsh, supports the method but sees some problems. "Not every family has a fast internet connection or a quiet place to study," she says. For this reason, the school now opens its computer room for an hour before lessons begin, so that students can watch the videos there. Mrs Marsh also points out that flipped lessons do not suit every subject. "They work very well in maths and science," she says, "but our art and sports teachers have not found them helpful."
What do researchers think? Dr Laura Benton, from a university in Scotland, followed students at twelve schools for three years. She found that test results were a little better, on average, in flipped classes. The biggest improvement was among weaker students, perhaps because they received more help from the teacher. However, Dr Benton warns that the video is not the important part. "If the teacher just hands out worksheets in class, nothing has really changed," she says. "What matters most is what students do in the classroom." She also believes that the method is more suitable for teenagers than for young children, who often find it hard to work without an adult.
At Brookside, the experiment will continue. When the school asked parents for their opinion, most of them said they were happy with the new lessons, although some were worried at first about the extra time their children spent looking at screens. Next year, the school plans to use the method in history and geography as well. The flipped classroom is not magic, but it has given teachers like Mr Osei something valuable: time to teach each student.

READING PASSAGE 2
TURNING THE CLASSROOM UPSIDE DOWN
In a "flipped" classroom, students meet new ideas at home and practise them at school

In a traditional lesson, the teacher stands at the front of the room and explains a new topic. The students listen and take notes. Later, at home, they practise alone by doing homework. This pattern has hardly changed for more than a hundred years. In a "flipped classroom", however, the order is turned upside down. Students first meet new ideas at home, usually by watching a short video. Class time is then used for practice, with the teacher there to help.
The idea became widely known after 2007, when two teachers at a school in Colorado, in the United States, began to record their chemistry lessons. At first, the recordings were only for students who had been absent. But the teachers soon noticed something interesting: students who had been in class were watching the videos too, because they wanted to go over the lesson again. Since then, schools in many countries have tried the method.
How does a flipped lesson work? David Osei, who teaches maths at Brookside School in the north of England, describes his week. First, he records a video of about ten minutes and puts it on the school website. At home, his students watch the video. They can stop it or repeat any part, and they write down any questions they have. They then complete a short online quiz. Before the lesson, Mr Osei looks at the results of the quiz to see which points were difficult. In class, there is a short discussion of the students' questions. After that, the students solve problems in small groups, while the teacher walks around the room and helps anyone who is stuck. Finally, the students write a summary of what they have learned in their notebooks.
Mr Osei says the biggest change is in how he uses his time. "I used to talk for forty minutes while thirty students sat in silence," he says. "Now I speak to every student at least once in each lesson." He admits, however, that the method was hard work at the start. "In the first year, I spent most of my weekends making videos," he says.
The students have noticed a difference too. Sofia Rossi, who is fifteen, likes being able to watch the difficult parts again. "In a normal lesson, I was too shy to ask the teacher to repeat something," she explains. "With a video, I can play it three times and nobody knows." But she adds that the system only works if everyone prepares. "Some of my classmates don't watch the videos," she says, "and then they can't join in the group work."
The head teacher of Brookside, Helen Marsh, supports the method but sees some problems. "Not every family has a fast internet connection or a quiet place to study," she says. For this reason, the school now opens its computer room for an hour before lessons begin, so that students can watch the videos there. Mrs Marsh also points out that flipped lessons do not suit every subject. "They work very well in maths and science," she says, "but our art and sports teachers have not found them helpful."
What do researchers think? Dr Laura Benton, from a university in Scotland, followed students at twelve schools for three years. She found that test results were a little better, on average, in flipped classes. The biggest improvement was among weaker students, perhaps because they received more help from the teacher. When the school asked parents for their opinion, most of them said they were happy with the new lessons, although some were worried at first about the extra time their children spent looking at screens. Next year, the school plans to use the method in history and geography as well. The flipped classroom is not magic, but it has given teachers like Mr Osei something valuable: time to teach each student.

nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 3
THE BARCODE: LINES THAT CHANGED SHOPPING
How an idea drawn in the sand ended up on almost every product in the world

Look at almost any product in a shop – a carton of milk, a book, a pair of shoes – and you will find a small square of black and white lines. A machine reads this barcode in less than a second, with a short "beep". We hear that sound so often that we no longer notice it. Yet the barcode took more than twenty-five years to travel from an idea to the supermarket.
The story begins in 1948 in Philadelphia, in the United States. A student called Bernard Silver happened to hear a conversation at his college. The president of a local supermarket company was asking a senior person at the college for help. His shops needed a way to record each product automatically when customers paid, because typing every price by hand was slow and caused mistakes. The college was not interested, but Silver was. He described the problem to his friend Norman Joseph Woodland, and the two young men decided to work on it together.
Woodland found the answer in an unusual place. He had moved to Florida, and one day he was sitting on a beach, thinking about Morse code, the system of dots and dashes that he had learned as a boy. He pushed his fingers into the sand and pulled them towards him, drawing a set of lines. Suddenly he understood: thin and thick lines could carry information in the same way as dots and dashes. In 1952, they received a patent for their invention. It showed a set of straight lines, but it also showed a second design that was not made of lines at all. It was a set of circles, one inside another, like a target. The advantage of this shape was that a machine could read it from any direction.
Unfortunately, the invention was ahead of its time. To read the code, a shop needed a small, strong light and a cheap computer, and neither existed in the early 1950s. The solution to the first problem was the laser, which was not invented until 1960. Woodland and Silver sold their patent for only 15,000 dollars, and Silver died in 1963 without ever seeing a barcode in a shop.
In the early 1970s, American supermarkets finally agreed that all their products should carry the same kind of code. The design they chose came from the computer company IBM, where Woodland now worked. It used straight lines instead of circles, because lines were easier to print clearly on packets. On 26 June 1974, in a supermarket in the town of Troy, Ohio, the new system was used for the first time. The first product to be scanned was a packet of chewing gum, which cost 67 cents. That packet of gum was later given to a museum in Washington.
The barcode did not become popular overnight. Scanners were expensive, so shops did not want to buy them until most products had codes. Food companies, on the other hand, did not want to print codes until most shops had scanners. For several years, the system spread very slowly. Some customers were unhappy too. When barcodes arrived, shops stopped putting a price label on every item, and shoppers complained that they could no longer check what they were paying. In the end, though, the advantages were clear. Queues moved faster, there were fewer mistakes, and for the first time managers knew exactly what they had sold and what they needed to order.
In 1994, a Japanese engineer called Masahiro Hara took the idea a step further. His company made parts for cars, and every box of parts in its factories carried a barcode. But an ordinary barcode can only hold about twenty letters or numbers. This was not enough information, so workers had to scan several codes on every box. Hara's answer was a square pattern of black and white dots that could hold thousands of characters. He called it the QR code – QR means "quick response". Three large squares in its corners tell the scanner where the code begins, so it can be read at high speed from any angle. Hara has said that the idea for the pattern came from the black and white stones of a board game that he played in his lunch breaks.
Hara's company decided that the QR code should be free to use, and it did not ask other companies for money. At first, the code was used mainly in factories. Everything changed when mobile phones with cameras appeared. Suddenly anyone could read a QR code, and the pattern began to appear on posters, tickets and bills. During 2020 and 2021, many restaurants even replaced their paper menus with a QR code on the table. More than fifty years after that first packet of chewing gum, black and white patterns are part of everyday life – and most of us never think about the people who invented them.

In 1994, a Japanese engineer called Masahiro Hara took the idea a step further. His company made parts for cars, and every box of parts in its factories carried a barcode. But an ordinary barcode can only hold about twenty letters or numbers. This was not enough information, so workers had to scan several codes on every box. Hara's answer was a square pattern of black and white dots that could hold thousands of characters. He called it the QR code – QR means "quick response". Three large squares in its corners tell the scanner where the code begins, so it can be read at high speed from any angle. Hara has said that the idea for the pattern came from the black and white stones of a board game that he played in his lunch breaks.
Hara's company decided that the QR code should be free to use, and it did not ask other companies for money. At first, the code was used mainly in factories. Everything changed when mobile phones with cameras appeared. Suddenly anyone could read a QR code, and the pattern began to appear on posters, tickets and bills. During 2020 and 2021, many restaurants even replaced their paper menus with a QR code on the table. More than fifty years after that first packet of chewing gum, black and white patterns are part of everyday life – and most of us never think about the people who invented them.
